t: The Linear Pottery culture spread about 1,500 km along the rivers in 360 years, about 4 km a year, and represents a major event in the spread of agriculture in Europe.
Its longhouses, 5.5 to 7.0 m wide and sometimes 45 m long, were the largest free-standing buildings in the world at the time.
Mass graves such as the Talheim Death Pit and Herxheim overturned an earlier view of the culture as peaceful and unfortified.
dyk: A 2022 study of residues from over 4,300 vessels at 70 LBK sites found traces of milk at about 65% of them, some dating as early as 7,400 years ago.
ev: The early Linear Pottery culture developed on the middle Danube, possibly as early as 5700 BCE
The classical Alföld Linear Pottery culture appeared north of the Körös culture
The LBK reached the Netherlands while Music Note pottery appeared in Austria
The settlement at Vráble reached its peak with perhaps 70 longhouses and up to 1,725 people
The killings of the Talheim Death Pit took place, among the earliest evidence of organised violence in Neolithic Europe
Stroke-ornamented ware developed in central Europe and spread down the Vistula and Elbe
A timber trackway was laid across the Campemoor bog in Lower Saxony

f.homeland: Central Europe, chiefly the middle Danube, the upper and middle Elbe and the upper and middle Rhine, at its widest from the Paris Basin to the Dnieper; key sites include Vráble and Nitra in Slovakia, Bylany in the Czech Republic, Langweiler and Zwenkau (Eythra) in Germany, Brunn am Gebirge in Austria, Elsloo in the Netherlands and Flomborn, Hienheim and Rössen
f.period: Early or Western LBK from conventionally 5500 BCE (possibly 5700 BCE); Music Note pottery from about 5200 BCE; Stroke-ornamented ware 5000–4500 BCE; the Eastern or Alföld LBK c. 5330–4940 BCE; a late survival in Belgium as late as 4100 BCE
f.known: incised “linear band” pottery; timber longhouses up to 45 m long; the rapid spread of farming at about 4 km a year; emmer and einkorn wheat, peas and lentils; cattle and dairying; timber-lined wells; the mass graves of Talheim, Herxheim and Schöneck-Kilianstädten
f.sources: Excavated settlements, cemeteries and wells; radiocarbon dates; the term Bandkeramik from Friedrich Klopfleisch and V. Gordon Childe’s Danubian; ancient DNA studies from 2005 onward; residue analysis of over 4,300 pots; the interpretations of Marija Gimbutas
